title: JEE Main Question Bank – Coordinate Geometry 01 — Paper Analysis
subtitle: Straight Line (Q1–Q20) · detailed solutions

sections.title: Single Correct Type
marking: 4 marks each (JEE Advanced default; no marks printed in the paper)

concepts: Intercepts and area of the triangle cut off by a line
Perpendicular from the origin to a line
questions.question: Let the area of the triangle formed by a straight line $L: x+by+c=0$ with the co-ordinate axes be $48$ square units. If the perpendicular drawn from the origin to the line $L$ makes an angle of $45^\circ$ with the positive $x$-axis, then the value of $b^2+c^2$ is:
questions.key_idea: The perpendicular from the origin has the direction of the normal $(1,b)$, so a $45^\circ$ angle forces $b=1$.
solution: The line meets the axes at $(-c,0)$ and $\left(0,-\frac{c}{b}\right)$.
Area of the triangle $=\frac12\left|(-c)\left(-\frac cb\right)\right|=48$, so $\left|\frac{c^2}{b}\right|=96$ ...(1).
Slope of $L$ is $-\frac1b$, so the slope of the perpendicular to $L$ (the perpendicular from the origin) is $b$.
This perpendicular makes $45^\circ$ with the positive $x$-axis, so $b=\tan45^\circ=1$.

alternate_solutions.idea: A $45^\circ$ normal means equal intercepts, so the triangle with the axes is an isosceles right triangle with legs $|c|$.
solution: The perpendicular from the origin is along the normal vector $(1,b)$ of $L$; it makes $45^\circ$ with the positive $x$-axis, so $(1,b)\parallel(1,1)$ and $b=1$.
Then $L: x+y+c=0$ has intercepts $-c$ and $-c$ on the two axes, so the triangle is an isosceles right triangle with both legs $|c|$.

useful_results: For $ax+by+c=0$ with $a,b,c\neq0$ the intercepts are $-\frac ca$ and $-\frac cb$, and the area cut off with the axes is $\frac{c^2}{2|ab|}$.
The foot of the perpendicular from the origin lies along the normal vector $(a,b)$, so its inclination is $\tan^{-1}\frac ba$; here it is $45^\circ$ exactly when $a=b$, i.e. equal intercepts.
Instance: $a=b=1$, $c^2=96$; check: area $=\frac{96}{2}=48$.

concepts: Angle between two lines
Distance between parallel lines
questions.question: A line passes through the origin and makes equal angles with the positive coordinate axes. It intersects the lines $L_1: 2x+y+6=0$ and $L_2: 4x+2y-p=0$, $p>0$, at the points $A$ and $B$, respectively. If $AB=\frac{9}{\sqrt2}$ and the foot of the perpendicular from the point $A$ on the line $L_2$ is $M$, then $\frac{AM}{BM}$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: $L_1\parallel L_2$, so $AM\perp L_2$ and $\frac{AM}{BM}=\tan$ of the angle between the line $y=x$ and $L_2$.
solution: A line through the origin making equal angles with the positive axes is $y=x$, of slope $m_1=1$.
$L_2: 4x+2y-p=0$ has slope $m_2=-2$ (and $L_1$ also has slope $-2$, so $L_1\parallel L_2$).
$AM\perp L_2$ with $M$ on $L_2$ and $B$ on $L_2$, so $\triangle AMB$ is right-angled at $M$, and $\angle ABM=\theta$ (the angle between $AB$, which lies on $y=x$, and $L_2$).
Consistency check: $A=(-2,-2)$, $B=\left(\frac p6,\frac p6\right)$, $AB=\sqrt2\left(\frac p6+2\right)=\frac9{\sqrt2}$ gives $p=15>0$; the value of $AB$ is not needed for the ratio.

alternate_solutions.idea: Since $L_1\parallel L_2$, $AM$ is the distance between the parallels; then $BM$ follows from Pythagoras in $\triangle ABM$.

useful_results: Angle between lines of slopes $m_1,m_2$: $\tan\theta=\left|\frac{m_1-m_2}{1+m_1m_2}\right|$ (valid when $1+m_1m_2\neq0$).

If a transversal meets two parallel lines at $A$ and $B$, and $M$ is the foot of the perpendicular from $A$ to the second line, then $\frac{AM}{BM}=\tan\theta$ where $\theta$ is the angle between the transversal and the parallels, whatever the gap between the lines.
Distance between $ax+by+c_1=0$ and $ax+by+c_2=0$ is $\frac{|c_1-c_2|}{\sqrt{a^2+b^2}}$ (coefficients of $x,y$ must be made equal first).

concepts: Equal roots of a quadratic equation
Distance of a point from a line
questions.question: Let the equation $x(x+2)(12-k)=2$ have equal roots. Then the distance of the point $\left(k,\frac k2\right)$ from the line $3x+4y+5=0$ is:
questions.key_idea: Put $12-k=\lambda$ to get $\lambda x^2+2\lambda x-2=0$; equal roots need $D=0$ with $\lambda\neq0$.
solution: The equation becomes $\lambda x^2+2\lambda x-2=0$ with $\lambda\neq0$ (i.e. $k\neq12$), so it is a genuine quadratic.

alternate_solutions.idea: $x^2+2x$ has minimum value $-1$ at its vertex, so $(x^2+2x)=t$ has equal roots only for $t=-1$.
solution: The parabola $y=x^2+2x=(x+1)^2-1$ touches the horizontal line $y=t$ exactly when $t=-1$ (equal roots $x=-1$).
The point is $(14,7)$ and the distance from $3x+4y+5=0$ is $\frac{42+28+5}{5}=15$.

useful_results: $x^2+2px+q=t$ has equal roots iff $t=q-p^2$ (the vertex value), so a 'parameter = constant' equation of this form needs no discriminant.

Distance of $(x_0,y_0)$ from $ax+by+c=0$ is $\frac{|ax_0+by_0+c|}{\sqrt{a^2+b^2}}$; with $3,4$ in the line the denominator is $5$ (3-4-5), so the numerator is divisible by $5$ in well-designed questions.
Instance: $\lambda x^2+2\lambda x-2=0$ has $D=4\lambda^2+8\lambda$; $D=0$ gives $\lambda=-2$, i.e. $\frac{2}{\lambda}=-1$.

concepts: Family of lines through the intersection of two lines
Distance of a point from a line
questions.question: Consider the lines $x(3\lambda+1)+y(7\lambda+2)=17\lambda+5$, $\lambda$ being a parameter, all passing through a point $P$. One of these lines (say $L$) is farthest from the origin. If the distance of $L$ from the point $(3,6)$ is $d$, then the value of $d^2$ is:
questions.key_idea: Among lines through $P$, the farthest from the origin is the one perpendicular to $OP$.
solution: Regroup in $\lambda$: $(x+2y-5)+\lambda(3x+7y-17)=0$, so every line passes through the intersection of $x+2y-5=0$ and $3x+7y-17=0$.
Of all lines through $P$, the one farthest from the origin is perpendicular to $OP$, and its distance is $OP$.
Let $Q=(3,6)$. Then $\overrightarrow{PQ}=(2,4)=2(1,2)=2\overrightarrow{OP}$, so $PQ\parallel OP$ and therefore $PQ\perp L$.
The foot of the perpendicular from $Q$ to $L$ is then $P$ itself, so $d=PQ$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Write the farthest line explicitly: through $P(1,2)$ with normal along $OP$, then apply the point-to-line distance formula.
solution: $P=(1,2)$ as before; the farthest line is perpendicular to $OP$, so its normal is $(1,2)$.
$L: 1(x-1)+2(y-2)=0$, i.e. $x+2y-5=0$ (this is the member of the family with $\lambda=0$).

useful_results: $L_1+\lambda L_2=0$ is the family of all lines through $L_1\cap L_2$ (except $L_2$ itself); read off the fixed point by solving $L_1=L_2=0$.
Among all lines through a point $P$, the distance from a fixed point $O$ is greatest ($=OP$) for the line through $P$ perpendicular to $OP$, and zero for the line through $O$.
Distance of $Q$ from the line through $P$ with normal $\vec n$ is $\frac{|\overrightarrow{PQ}\cdot\vec n|}{|\vec n|}$; it equals $PQ$ when $PQ\parallel\vec n$.

concepts: Orthocentre of a triangle
Slopes of perpendicular lines
questions.question: Let the three sides of a triangle be on the lines $4x-7y+10=0$, $x+y=5$ and $7x+4y=15$. Then the distance of its orthocentre from the orthocentre of the triangle formed by the lines $x=0$, $y=0$ and $x+y=1$ is:
questions.key_idea: Slopes $\frac47$ and $-\frac74$ multiply to $-1$, so the triangle is right-angled and its orthocentre is the right-angle vertex.
solution: Slope of $4x-7y+10=0$ is $\frac47$; slope of $7x+4y=15$ is $-\frac74$. Their product is $-1$, so these two sides are perpendicular.
Hence the triangle has a right angle at their common vertex.
In a right-angled triangle the orthocentre is the vertex of the right angle.
For the lines $x=0$, $y=0$, $x+y=1$: $x=0$ and $y=0$ are perpendicular, so the right angle is at the origin and the orthocentre is $(0,0)$.
useful_results: Lines $ax+by+c=0$ and $a'x+b'y+c'=0$ are perpendicular iff $aa'+bb'=0$ (here $4\cdot7+(-7)\cdot4=0$).
Right-angled triangle: orthocentre = right-angle vertex, circumcentre = midpoint of the hypotenuse; always test the sides' slopes for $m_1m_2=-1$ before computing altitudes.
Check: $(1,2)$ lies on the first and third lines ($4-14+10=0$, $7+8=15$) but not on $x+y=5$, so the triangle is non-degenerate.

concepts: Sum of binomial coefficients
Distance of a point from a line
questions.question: For an integer $n\ge2$, if the arithmetic mean of all coefficients in the binomial expansion of $(x+y)^{2n-3}$ is $16$, then the distance of the point $P(2n-1,\,n^2-4n)$ from the line $x+y=8$ is:
questions.key_idea: The expansion has $2n-2$ coefficients with sum $2^{2n-3}$; the equation $2^{2n-8}=n-1$ has the single integer root $n=5$.
solution: $(x+y)^{2n-3}$ has $2n-2$ terms and the sum of its binomial coefficients is $2^{2n-3}$.
By trial $n=5$: $2^2=4=5-1$. It is the only root: $n=2,3,4$ give $2^{-4},2^{-2},2^0$ against $1,2,3$, and for $n\ge6$ the left side ($\times4$ per step) outgrows the right side ($+1$ per step).

alternate_solutions.idea: Let $N=2n-2$ be the number of terms; then $2^{N-1}=16N$ is solved by a monotonic-growth argument.
solution: Set $N=2n-2$ (even, $N\ge2$). The sum of coefficients is $2^{N-1}$ and the mean is $\frac{2^{N-1}}{N}=16$.
The ratio is strictly increasing for $N\ge2$ since $\frac{2^{N}/(N+1)}{2^{N-1}/N}=\frac{2N}{N+1}>1$, so $N=8$ is the only solution.

useful_results: $(x+y)^N$ has $N+1$ coefficients with sum $2^N$ (put $x=y=1$); their mean is $\frac{2^N}{N+1}$.

Equations mixing $2^{\text{linear}}$ and linear terms have few integer roots; test small values and justify uniqueness by growth (the exponential side is multiplied each step, the linear side only increases by a constant).
Distance of $(x_0,y_0)$ from $x+y=c$ is $\frac{|x_0+y_0-c|}{\sqrt2}$; here $P=(9,5)$ gives $\frac6{\sqrt2}$.

concepts: Orthocentre of a triangle
Area of a triangle
questions.question: Let $ABC$ be the triangle such that the equations of lines $AB$ and $AC$ are $3y-x=2$ and $x+y=2$, respectively, and the points $B$ and $C$ lie on the $x$-axis. If $P$ is the orthocentre of the triangle $ABC$, then the area of the triangle $PBC$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: With $BC$ on the $x$-axis, the altitude from $A$ is the vertical line through $A$, so $H$ has $x=x_A$.
solution: $B$ is on $AB$ and the $x$-axis: $y=0$ in $3y-x=2$ gives $B=(-2,0)$.
$C$ is on $AC$ and the $x$-axis: $y=0$ in $x+y=2$ gives $C=(2,0)$.
Altitude from $A$ is perpendicular to $BC$ (the $x$-axis): the line $x=1$.
Altitude from $B$ is perpendicular to $AC$ (slope $-1$), so it has slope $1$: $y=x+2$.
At $x=1$ this gives $y=3$, so the orthocentre is $P=H(1,3)$.

alternate_solutions.idea: For a base on the $x$-axis, $B(b,0)$, $C(c,0)$ and apex $A(a,k)$, the orthocentre is $H=\left(a,\,-\frac{(a-b)(a-c)}{k}\right)$.

useful_results: If $B(b,0)$, $C(c,0)$, $A(a,k)$ then $H=\left(a,-\frac{(a-b)(a-c)}{k}\right)$: the altitude from $B$ has slope $\frac{c-a}{k}$ (perpendicular to $AC$), so at $x=a$ it gives $y=\frac{(c-a)(a-b)}{k}$. Check: $a=1$, $b=-2$, $c=2$, $k=1$ gives $y_H=3$.
Area of $\triangle HBC=\frac12|BC|\,|y_H|$; $H$ lies inside the triangle exactly when the triangle is acute.
Reflection of $H$ in side $BC$ lies on the circumcircle (here $(1,-3)$).

concepts: Orthocentre of a triangle
Equation of a line and its slope
questions.question: If the orthocentre of the triangle formed by the lines $y=x+1$, $y=4x-8$ and $y=mx+c$ is at $(3,-1)$, then $m-c$ is:
questions.key_idea: The vertex $A=(3,4)$ and the orthocentre $(3,-1)$ share $x=3$, so the altitude from $A$ is vertical and the third side is horizontal ($m=0$).
solution: Vertex $A$ is the meet of $y=x+1$ and $y=4x-8$: $x+1=4x-8$, so $A=(3,4)$.
The altitude from $A$ passes through the orthocentre $(3,-1)$, so it is the vertical line $x=3$ (slope $\infty$).
Hence side $BC$ ($y=mx+c$) is horizontal: $m=0$ and $BC: y=c$.
The altitude from $C$ goes to $E(3,-1)$: its slope is $\frac{c+1}{\frac{8+c}{4}-3}=\frac{4c+4}{c-4}$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Use the altitude from $B$ instead, written as the dot-product condition $\overrightarrow{BH}\cdot\overrightarrow{AC}=0$.
solution: $A=(3,4)$, $H=(3,-1)$ and the vertical altitude from $A$ give $m=0$, $B=(c-1,c)$, $C=\left(\frac{8+c}4,c\right)$.
$c=4$ would make $BC$ pass through $A$ (no triangle), so $\frac{c-4}{4}+c+1=0$, i.e. $5c=0$ and $c=0$.

useful_results: $H$ is the orthocentre iff $\overrightarrow{HA}\cdot\overrightarrow{BC}=0$ and $\overrightarrow{HB}\cdot\overrightarrow{CA}=0$ (the third relation follows).
If a vertex and the orthocentre have the same $x$-coordinate, the opposite side is horizontal; same $y$-coordinate means the opposite side is vertical.
Check: $A(3,4)$, $B(-1,0)$, $C(2,0)$, $H(3,-1)$: $\overrightarrow{BH}\cdot\overrightarrow{AC}=(4,-1)\cdot(-1,-4)=0$ and $\overrightarrow{CH}\cdot\overrightarrow{AB}=(1,-1)\cdot(-4,-4)=0$.

concepts: Square: diagonals and side length
Distance of a point from a line
questions.question: Let $a$ be the length of a side of a square $OABC$ with $O$ being the origin. Its side $OA$ makes an acute angle $\alpha$ with the positive $x$-axis and the equations of its diagonals are $\left(\sqrt3+1\right)x+\left(\sqrt3-1\right)y=0$ and $\left(\sqrt3-1\right)x-\left(\sqrt3+1\right)y+8\sqrt3=0$. Then $a^2$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: The diagonals are perpendicular and the first passes through $O$, so the centre is the foot of the perpendicular from $O$ on the second diagonal; $a^2=2\,OP^2$.
solution: $O$ is a vertex, so the diagonal through $O$, $(\sqrt3+1)x+(\sqrt3-1)y=0$, is $OB$; the other diagonal is $AC$.
Solve the two diagonals for their intersection, the centre $P$ of the square.
In the right triangle $OPA$ (diagonals meet at $90^\circ$): $OA^2=OP^2+PA^2$ with $PA=OP$.

alternate_solutions.idea: The two diagonals are perpendicular, so $OP$ is just the distance from $O$ to the second diagonal; no intersection point is needed.
solution: Normals: $(\sqrt3+1,\sqrt3-1)\cdot(\sqrt3-1,-(\sqrt3+1))=0$, so the diagonals are perpendicular.
The first passes through $O$, so the foot of the perpendicular from $O$ on the second diagonal is their intersection $P$.
The diagonal $OB=2\,OP=4\sqrt6$ and the side is $a=\frac{OB}{\sqrt2}$, so $a^2=\frac{96}{2}=48$.

useful_results: In a square of side $a$: diagonal $=a\sqrt2$, the diagonals are equal, perpendicular and bisect each other, so $a^2=2\,(\text{half-diagonal})^2$.

If one diagonal passes through a vertex $O$ and the other is perpendicular to it, the centre is the foot of the perpendicular from $O$ on the other diagonal, so the half-diagonal is a point-to-line distance.
Check: the centre $(\sqrt3-3,3+\sqrt3)$ satisfies both diagonals: $(\sqrt3+1)(\sqrt3-3)+(\sqrt3-1)(\sqrt3+3)=-2\sqrt3+2\sqrt3=0$.

concepts: Rotation of a line and its slope
Distance of a point from a line
questions.question: A line passing through the point $P(a,0)$ makes an acute angle $\alpha$ with the positive $x$-axis. Let this line be rotated about the point $P$ through an angle $\frac\alpha2$ in the clock-wise direction. If in the new position, the slope of the line is $2-\sqrt3$ and its distance from the origin is $\frac1{\sqrt2}$, then the value of $3a^2\tan^2\alpha-2\sqrt3$ is:
questions.key_idea: A clockwise rotation by $\frac\alpha2$ leaves inclination $\frac\alpha2$, so $\tan\frac\alpha2=2-\sqrt3=\tan15^\circ$ and $\alpha=30^\circ$.
solution: The clockwise rotation by $\frac\alpha2$ reduces the inclination from $\alpha$ to $\alpha-\frac\alpha2=\frac\alpha2$.

alternate_solutions.idea: A line through $(a,0)$ with inclination $15^\circ$ is at distance $|a|\sin15^\circ$ from the origin, which gives $a^2$ in one step.
solution: As above the new inclination is $15^\circ$ and $\alpha=30^\circ$.
The distance from the origin to a line through $(a,0)$ with inclination $\phi$ is $|a|\sin\phi$ (the origin and $P$ are on the $x$-axis).

useful_results: A line through $(a,0)$ with inclination $\phi$ has distance $|a\sin\phi|$ from the origin; through $(0,b)$ the distance is $|b\cos\phi|$.
$\tan15^\circ=2-\sqrt3$ and $\tan75^\circ=2+\sqrt3$; also $\sin^215^\circ=\frac{2-\sqrt3}{4}$.
Rotating a line anticlockwise by $\beta$ adds $\beta$ to its inclination; clockwise subtracts $\beta$ (slope $\tan(\phi\pm\beta)$).

concepts: Reflection (image) of a point in a line
Centroid of a triangle
questions.question: Let the triangle $PQR$ be the image of the triangle with vertices $(1,3)$, $(3,1)$ and $(2,4)$ in the line $x+2y=2$. If the centroid of $\triangle PQR$ is the point $(\alpha,\beta)$, then $15(\alpha-\beta)$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Reflection is an isometry, so the centroid of the image triangle is the image of the original centroid.
solution: The image of a triangle's centroid under reflection is the centroid of the image triangle, so reflect only the centroid.

alternate_solutions.idea: Reflection in $x+2y=2$ changes $x-y$ by a simple multiple of the 'line value', so $\alpha-\beta$ can be computed directly.

useful_results: Reflection of $(x_0,y_0)$ in $ax+by+c=0$: $(x_0,y_0)-\frac{2(ax_0+by_0+c)}{a^2+b^2}(a,b)$.
A reflection maps lines to lines, preserves distances and ratios, so it maps midpoints, centroids and orthocentres of a triangle to those of the image triangle.
Check: $G=\left(2,\frac83\right)$ and its image $\left(-\frac2{15},-\frac85\right)$ have midpoint $\left(\frac{14}{15},\frac{8}{15}\right)$, which satisfies $x+2y=2$.

concepts: Orthocentre and centroid of a triangle
Area of a triangle
questions.question: Let the area of a $\triangle PQR$ with vertices $P(5,4)$, $Q(-2,4)$ and $R(a,b)$ be $35$ square units. If its orthocentre and centroid are $O\left(2,\frac{14}5\right)$ and $C(c,d)$ respectively, then $c+2d$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: $PQ$ is horizontal, so the altitude from $R$ is vertical and $a=2$; then $OP\perp QR$ fixes $b$.
solution: The altitude from $R$ is perpendicular to $PQ$, hence vertical, and passes through $O(2,\frac{14}5)$: $a=2$, $R=(2,b)$.
$OP\perp QR$: $\frac25\cdot\frac{b-4}{4}=-1$, so $b-4=-10$ and $b=-6$ (the value $b=14$ is rejected).

alternate_solutions.idea: Use the closed formula $H=\left(a,\,y_0-\frac{(a-x_1)(a-x_2)}{b-y_0}\right)$ for a horizontal base on $y=y_0$.
solution: Base $PQ$ lies on $y_0=4$ with $x_1=5$, $x_2=-2$; apex $R=(a,b)$. The orthocentre has $x=a$, so $a=2$.
So $\frac{12}{b-4}=-\frac65$, giving $b-4=-10$ and $b=-6$ (and $|b-4|=10$ agrees with the area).

useful_results: For base $(x_1,y_0)$, $(x_2,y_0)$ and apex $(a,b)$: $H=\left(a,\,y_0-\frac{(a-x_1)(a-x_2)}{b-y_0}\right)$; the sign of $y_H-y_0$ tells whether $H$ is on the apex side.
Area from base and height: $\frac12\cdot\text{base}\cdot|b-y_0|$ avoids the determinant when a side is axis-parallel and always gives two candidate positions ($\pm$) for the apex.
The orthocentre condition then picks one: here $b=14$ would give $y_H=4+\frac{12}{10}=\frac{26}5\neq\frac{14}5$.

concepts: Locus of a point dividing a moving segment
Section formula
questions.question: A rod of length eight units moves such that its ends $A$ and $B$ always lie on the lines $x-y+2=0$ and $y+2=0$, respectively. If the locus of the point $P$, that divides the rod $AB$ internally in the ratio $2:1$ is $9\left(x^2+\alpha y^2+\beta xy+\gamma x+28y\right)-76=0$, then $\alpha-\beta-\gamma$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Write $A=(\lambda,\lambda+2)$, $B=(\mu,-2)$, express $\lambda,\mu$ through $P=(h,k)$ by the section formula, and substitute in $AB^2=64$.
solution: Let $A=(\lambda,\lambda+2)$ on $x-y+2=0$ and $B=(\mu,-2)$ on $y+2=0$; let $P=(h,k)$ divide $AB$ in the ratio $2:1$, so $P=\frac{A+2B}{3}$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Parametrise the rod by its inclination $\varphi$: $\vec{BA}=8(\cos\varphi,\sin\varphi)$, then eliminate $\varphi$ with $\sin^2\varphi+\cos^2\varphi=1$.
solution: This is the same locus $9\left[x^2+13y^2-6xy-4x+28y\right]-76=0$, so $\alpha-\beta-\gamma=23$.

useful_results: Locus of a point dividing a rod of fixed length that slides with its ends on two lines: express both end-parameters through $(h,k)$ with the section formula, then use the length condition; the locus is a conic (here an ellipse, since $B^2-4AC=36-52<0$).
If $P$ divides $AB$ in the ratio $AP:PB=m:n$ then $P=\frac{nA+mB}{m+n}$; for $2:1$, $P=\frac{A+2B}{3}$.
Check: rod vertical, $B=(4,-2)$, $A=(4,6)$ (on $x-y+2=0$, $AB=8$); $P=\left(4,\frac23\right)$ and $9\left(16+\frac{52}9-16-16+\frac{56}3\right)=76$.

concepts: Concurrent lines
Reflection (image) of a point in a line
questions.question: Let the lines $3x-4y-\alpha=0$, $8x-11y-33=0$, and $2x-3y+\lambda=0$ be concurrent. If the image of the point $(1,2)$ in the line $2x-3y+\lambda=0$ is $\left(\frac{57}{13},\frac{-40}{13}\right)$, then $|\alpha\lambda|$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: The line $2x-3y+\lambda=0$ is the perpendicular bisector of the point and its image, so the midpoint lies on it; concurrency gives a determinant condition.
solution: Let $P(1,2)$ and its image $Q\left(\frac{57}{13},\frac{-40}{13}\right)$. The mirror $2x-3y+\lambda=0$ passes through the midpoint $M$ of $PQ$.
questions.correction_note: In the PDF's expanded line it writes '33λ − 297 + 32λ + 264 + 24α − 22α = 0'. The first term should be −33λ (from 3(−11λ − 99)) and the α terms combine to +2α (−α(−24+22)); with these the line gives −λ + 2α − 33 = 0 as the PDF concludes. The final answer 91 is unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: Find the common point of the two fixed lines $8x-11y=33$ and $2x-3y=7$ and feed it to the first line, avoiding the determinant.
solution: The perpendicular bisector property gives $\lambda=-7$ exactly as above (also: $\overrightarrow{PQ}=\left(\frac{44}{13},-\frac{66}{13}\right)=\frac{22}{13}(2,-3)$ is along the normal, a consistency check).
With $\lambda=-7$ the third line is $2x-3y=7$. The common point of $8x-11y=33$ and $2x-3y=7$: $8x-12y=28$, so $y=5$ and $x=11$.

useful_results: The mirror line is the perpendicular bisector of a point and its image: the midpoint lies on it and the segment is parallel to the normal $(a,b)$.
Three lines $a_ix+b_iy+c_i=0$ are concurrent iff $\det[a_i\ b_i\ c_i]=0$ (or: the meet of two lies on the third); with one parameter, solving the two simpler lines is often quicker than expanding.

concepts: Region represented by linear inequalities (points inside a triangle)
questions.question: Let the points $\left(\frac{11}2,\alpha\right)$ lie on or inside the triangle with sides $x+y=11$, $x+2y=16$ and $2x+3y=29$. Then the product of the smallest and the largest values of $\alpha$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Intersect the vertical line $x=\frac{11}{2}$ with the triangle: find the vertices first, then see which two sides it crosses.
solution: Vertices: $x+y=11$ and $x+2y=16$ meet at $Q(6,5)$; $x+y=11$ and $2x+3y=29$ meet at $R(4,7)$; $x+2y=16$ and $2x+3y=29$ meet at $P(10,3)$.
The line $x=\frac{11}2$ lies between $x=4$ (vertex $R$) and $x=6$ (vertex $Q$), so it cuts the two sides through $R$: $RQ$ ($x+y=11$) and $RP$ ($2x+3y=29$).
Hence $\frac{11}2\le\alpha\le6$, and the required product is $\frac{11}{2}\times6=33$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Describe the triangle by three inequalities, using a vertex opposite each side as the test point.
solution: Vertices $R(4,7)$, $Q(6,5)$, $P(10,3)$. Test the opposite vertex for each side.
Together $\frac{11}2\le\alpha\le6$ (the second inequality is not binding), so the product is $33$.

useful_results: A point is inside a triangle iff it is on the same side of each side-line as the opposite vertex; plug the vertex into $ax+by+c$ to decide the inequality's direction.
On a vertical line $x=x_0$ the range of $y$ inside the triangle is bounded by the two sides crossing $x_0$; the third side's inequality may be non-binding (here $\alpha\ge\frac{21}4<\frac{11}2$).
Instance check: $\left(\frac{11}2,\frac{11}2\right)$ is on $RQ$ and $\left(\frac{11}2,6\right)$ is on $RP$, both inside or on the triangle.

concepts: Angle between two lines
Isosceles triangle: slope of the base
questions.question: Two equal sides of an isosceles triangle are along $-x+2y=4$ and $x+y=4$. If $m$ is the slope of its third side, then the sum of all possible distinct values of $m$ is:
questions.key_idea: The base makes equal angles with the two equal sides, so $\left|\frac{m-m_1}{1+m_1m}\right|=\left|\frac{m-m_2}{1+m_2m}\right|$.
solution: Slopes of the equal sides: $-x+2y=4$ gives $m_1=\frac12$; $x+y=4$ gives $m_2=-1$.
The third side $y=mx+c$ makes equal base angles $\theta$ with them: $\left|\frac{m-m_1}{1+m_1m}\right|=\left|\frac{m-m_2}{1+m_2m}\right|$.
Sum of the distinct values $=6$ (also $m=1$, $m=-2$ and a vertical base do not work).

alternate_solutions.idea: The base of an isosceles triangle is perpendicular to an angle bisector of the two equal sides, so $m=-\frac1{\text{(bisector slope)}}$.
solution: Write the sides as $x-2y+4=0$ and $x+y-4=0$. The bisectors are $\frac{x-2y+4}{\sqrt5}=\pm\frac{x+y-4}{\sqrt2}$.
The base is perpendicular to a bisector: $m=-\frac1{s}$, so $m_1=\frac{2\sqrt2+\sqrt5}{\sqrt5-\sqrt2}$ and $m_2=\frac{\sqrt5-2\sqrt2}{\sqrt5+\sqrt2}$.

useful_results: Isosceles triangle with equal sides on lines $\ell_1,\ell_2$: the base is perpendicular to one of the two angle bisectors of $\ell_1,\ell_2$, giving two possible base directions.

The two bisectors satisfy $\frac{a_1x+b_1y+c_1}{\sqrt{a_1^2+b_1^2}}=\pm\frac{a_2x+b_2y+c_2}{\sqrt{a_2^2+b_2^2}}$; the slopes of the two possible bases are the roots of the quadratic from $\tan$-equality, so their sum is read from the coefficients (here $m^2-6m-1=0$).

Check: for $m=3+\sqrt{10}\approx6.162$, both $\left|\frac{m-1/2}{1+m/2}\right|$ and $\left|\frac{m+1}{1-m}\right|$ equal $\approx1.387$; for $m=3-\sqrt{10}\approx-0.162$ the moduli are both $\approx0.721$.

concepts: Centroid of a triangle
Reflection (image) of a point in a line
questions.question: Let $ABC$ be a triangle formed by the lines $7x-6y+3=0$, $x+2y-31=0$ and $9x-2y-19=0$. Let the point $(h,k)$ be the image of the centroid of $\triangle ABC$ in the line $3x+6y-53=0$. Then $h^2+k^2+hk$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Find the three vertices, take their average for the centroid, then use the reflection formula.

alternate_solutions.idea: Guess-and-verify: the image of $G$ is the vertex $(3,4)$, because the mirror is the perpendicular bisector of $G$ and that vertex.
solution: $\overrightarrow{GC}$ for $C=(3,4)$ is $\left(\frac83,\frac{16}3\right)=\frac83(1,2)$, which is parallel to the normal $(3,6)$ of the mirror.
The midpoint of $GC$ is $\left(\frac{13}3,\frac{20}3\right)$ and $3\cdot\frac{13}3+6\cdot\frac{20}3-53=13+40-53=0$, so it lies on the mirror.
A segment parallel to the normal whose midpoint is on the mirror is bisected perpendicularly by it, so the image of $G$ is $C=(3,4)$.

useful_results: Two points are mirror images in a line iff the segment joining them is parallel to the normal and its midpoint lies on the line; this lets one verify a guessed image in two lines.
Centroid of a triangle is the average of its vertices; vertices of a triangle given by three lines come from pairwise solving (three $2\times2$ systems).
Instance: $G=\left(\frac{17}3,\frac{28}3\right)$ has line value $17+56-53=20$, image $=G-\frac{2\cdot20}{45}(3,6)=(3,4)$.

concepts: Inscribed right-angled triangle in a triangle
Trigonometry in coordinate geometry
questions.question: Let the line $x+y=1$ meet the axes of $x$ and $y$ at $A$ and $B$, respectively. A right angled triangle $AMN$ is inscribed in the triangle $OAB$, where $O$ is the origin and the points $M$ and $N$ lie on the lines $OB$ and $AB$ respectively. If the area of the triangle $AMN$ is $\frac49$ of the area of the triangle $OAB$ and $AN:NB=\lambda:1$, then the sum of all possible value(s) of $\lambda$ is:
questions.key_idea: With the right angle at $N$ (as in the figure), $\triangle MNB$ is isosceles right, so $\frac{AN}{NB}=\frac{AN}{MN}=\cot\theta$ where $\theta=\angle MAN$.
solution: The right angle is at $N$ ($MN\perp AB$, $M$ on $OB$, $N$ on $AB$, as in the figure). Let $\angle MAN=\theta$; since $\angle OAB=45^\circ$, $\angle OAM=45^\circ-\theta$.
$\tan\theta=2$ means $\theta>45^\circ$, so $\angle OAM=45^\circ-\theta<0$: $M$ would not lie on $OB$ (not inscribed); it is rejected. Hence $\tan\theta=\frac12$.
In $\triangle MNB$: $\angle B=45^\circ$ and $\angle N=90^\circ$, so $NB=MN$. Therefore $\frac{AN}{NB}=\frac{AM\cos\theta}{AM\sin\theta}=\cot\theta=2$.
So $\lambda=2$ is the only possible value, and the sum is $2$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Coordinates: put $N=(1-t,t)$ on $AB$; then $MN\perp AB$ makes $M=(0,2t-1)$ and the area collapses to $t(1-t)$.
solution: $MN\perp AB$ means $MN$ is parallel to the normal $(1,1)$ of $AB$; $M$ is on $x=0$, so $M-N=(-(1-t),-(1-t))$ and $M=(0,\,2t-1)$. Also $MN=(1-t)\sqrt2$ (legs along $(1,1)$).
$\text{ar}(\triangle AMN)=\frac12\cdot AN\cdot MN=\frac12\cdot t\sqrt2\cdot(1-t)\sqrt2=t(1-t)=\frac29$, so $t=\frac13$ or $\frac23$.
$M$ must be on the segment $OB$, i.e. $2t-1\ge0$, so $t\ge\frac12$: $t=\frac23$ (for $t=\frac13$, $M=(0,-\frac13)$ is outside the triangle).

useful_results: For a point $N$ on the hypotenuse $AB$ of the right isosceles triangle $OAB$ ($\angle B=45^\circ$), the perpendicular to $AB$ at $N$ meeting $OB$ at $M$ gives $NB=NM$; so $\frac{AN}{NB}=\frac{AN}{NM}=\cot\angle MAN$.
'Inscribed' means the vertices lie on the sides themselves, which rejects the root that would put a vertex on the extended line.
With $N$ at fraction $t$ along $AB$ from $A$ (hypotenuse $\sqrt2$), the area of the right triangle $AMN$ (right angle at $N$) is $t(1-t)$; check $t=\frac23$: $\frac29$.

concepts: Distance between parallel lines (shifting a side)
Equation of the side of a triangle
questions.question: The vertices of a triangle are $A(-1,3)$, $B(-2,2)$ and $C(3,-1)$. A new triangle is formed by shifting the sides of the triangle by one unit inwards. Then the equation of the side of the new triangle nearest to origin is:
questions.key_idea: Decide the interior side of each line by testing the opposite vertex, shift the constant by $\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$ towards it, then compare distances from the origin.
solution: The PDF figure prints $B(2,2)$ and $C(3,1)$; the question's vertices are $A(-1,3)$, $B(-2,2)$, $C(3,-1)$ and are used here.
Interior side of each line (test the opposite vertex): $AB$ with $C$: $3+1+4>0$; $BC$ with $A$: $-3+15-4>0$; $AC$ with $B$: $-2+2-2<0$.
Shifting a line $ax+by+c=0$ by one unit changes $c$ by $\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$: new sides $x-y+4=\sqrt2$, $3x+5y-4=\sqrt{34}$ and $x+y-2=-\sqrt2$.
questions.correction_note: The PDF's figure labels B(2,2) and C(3,1) (the question has B(-2,2), C(3,-1)); it writes AB as 'x - y - 4 = 0' whereas the line through A(-1,3) and B(-2,2) is x - y + 4 = 0; it does not say which direction is 'inwards', and it gives the shifted constants (e.g. c = √2 - 4) without a comparison of distances. The answer (A) is correct and unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: Compare the origin's signed distances to the three sides first, so only the nearest shifted line has to be written.
solution: Lines (interior sign as in the main solution): $AB: x-y+4=0$ (interior $>0$), $BC: 3x+5y-4=0$ (interior $>0$), $AC: x+y-2=0$ (interior $<0$).
At the origin: $AB$ gives $+4$ (inside side, distance $\frac4{\sqrt2}=2\sqrt2$); $BC$ gives $-4$ (outside side, distance $\frac4{\sqrt{34}}$); $AC$ gives $-2$ (inside side, distance $\sqrt2$).
Moving a side one unit inwards changes its distance from the origin by $1$ in the direction of the interior: $2\sqrt2-1\approx1.83$, $\frac{4}{\sqrt{34}}+1\approx1.69$, $\sqrt2-1\approx0.41$.
The smallest is the shifted $AC$; its equation is $x+y-2=-\sqrt2$, i.e. $x+y-(2-\sqrt2)=0$.

useful_results: Shifting $ax+by+c=0$ by $d$ units towards a chosen side gives $ax+by+c=\pm d\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$; choose the sign by which side the target is on.
The interior of a triangle is the side of each line that contains the opposite vertex; a point's signed value $ax+by+c$ tells directly whether it is inside or outside.

The 'inner parallel triangle' at distance $d$ is similar to the original with ratio $\frac{r-d}{r}$ ($r$ = inradius). Here $r=\frac{8}{5\sqrt2+\sqrt{34}}\approx0.62<1$, so the one-unit shift overshoots the incentre and the shifted lines form an inverted triangle; the lines themselves are as computed.

concepts: Isosceles right triangle with vertex at the origin
Distance of a point from a line
questions.question: Let two straight lines drawn from the origin $O$ intersect the line $3x+4y=12$ at the points $P$ and $Q$ such that $\triangle OPQ$ is an isosceles triangle and $\angle POQ=90^\circ$. If $l=OP^2+PQ^2+QO^2$, then the greatest integer less than or equal to $l$ is:
questions.key_idea: $OP=OQ$ with $\angle POQ=90^\circ$, so each of $OP$, $OQ$ makes $45^\circ$ with the given line; find the two lines and the points $P$, $Q$.
solution: $\triangle OPQ$ is isosceles with the right angle at $O$, so $OP=OQ$ and $\angle OQP=45^\circ$: the line $OQ$ makes $45^\circ$ with $3x+4y=12$ (slope $-\frac34$).
Taking $+1$: $m+\frac34=1-\frac{3m}4$, so $\frac{7m}4=\frac14$ and $m=\frac17$ (taking $-1$ gives $m=-7$, the perpendicular line $OP$).
$l=\frac{288+288+576}{25}=\frac{1152}{25}=46.08$, so the greatest integer $\le l$ is $46$.
questions.correction_note: The PDF labels the line OP as 'y = 7x' although its own point P(-12/25, 84/25) (from -25x = 12) lies on y = -7x. Corrected to y = -7x; every later number and the answer 46 are unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: In an isosceles right triangle the altitude from the right-angle vertex is half the hypotenuse, so the distance from $O$ to the line gives everything.
solution: Distance from $O$ to $3x+4y=12$: $h=\frac{12}{5}$; this is the altitude from $O$ to the hypotenuse $PQ$.
In an isosceles right triangle with right angle at $O$, the altitude to the hypotenuse is half of it: $PQ=2h=\frac{24}5$.

useful_results: In a right isosceles triangle with the right angle at $O$ and hypotenuse $PQ$ on a line at distance $h$ from $O$: $PQ=2h$, $OP=OQ=h\sqrt2$, and $OP^2+PQ^2+QO^2=2PQ^2=8h^2$.
Instance: $h=\frac{12}5$ gives $8h^2=\frac{1152}{25}=46.08$.

The two lines from $O$ making $45^\circ$ with the given line have slopes $m$ with $\left|\frac{m-m_0}{1+m_0m}\right|=1$; they are perpendicular to each other, which is why they form the right angle at $O$.
